stories.headline: Sources: Man United turn to U.S. coach Pochettino with Carrick on the brink
stories.summary: United States coach Mauricio Pochettino is the favored candidate to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United manager, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
United States men's national team coach Mauricio Pochettino is the favored candidate to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United manager with the club ready to fire the 45-year-old due to growing alarm over the team dropping into the Premier League relegation zone, sources have told ESPN.

The United hierarchy, led by co-chairman Joel Glazer, minority owner Jim Ratcliffe, CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, is assessing Carrick's position after the club's worst-ever start to a Premier League season left United just one point off the bottom of the table having won once in 10 league games to date.

While sources have said discussions are ongoing and will continue over the coming days, they have also told ESPN that there is now acceptance that performances and results demand a change of manager.

- Ogden: Ratcliffe chose to appoint rookies at Man United, and it has them facing relegation﻿ fight

Pochettino, 54, extended his contract with the U.S. Soccer Federation until 2030 in August after guiding the United States to the round of 16 at the World Cup this summer.

According to multiple reports, the former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain coach has an escape clause in his new contract that would prevent United from having to pay a significant compensation fee for the Argentine's services.

Former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe is another candidate admired by United bosses. Julian Nagelsmann, who is also currently out of work, is among the options, and Kieran McKenna, who was interviewed for the job in 2024, has supporters at Old Trafford.

But it is Pochettino -- who has interviewed for the United job on three previous occasions -- who is regarded as having the Premier League experience and personality needed to drag United out of danger and revive the club's fortunes.

Carrick signed a two-year contract at United in the summer after guiding the club to Champions League qualification following his arrival as interim manager in January.

Sources have said that United believed Carrick, whose only previous managerial experience was with Championship team Middlesbrough, merited a long-term deal after his success at Old Trafford last season.

But senior figures have been shocked by the drop in performances and results this season. After they gave the former United midfielder time to turn around the situation last month, Carrick has been able to win only one of four games since his reprieve, and sources have said that his prospects are now increasingly bleak.

United are next in action against Liverpool at Anfield on Nov. 22.

- Neville on Carrick's Man United future: 'Ownership don't have a clue'

stories.headline: Doc Rivers says he apologized to Giannis Antetokounmpo while clarifying critiques
stories.summary: Doc Rivers said he reached out to apologize to Giannis Antetokounmpo for questioning his basketball IQ, saying he meant more that the force he plays with can get "in the way of his feel."
stories.body:
Former Milwaukee Bucks head coach Doc Rivers told ESPN Andscape on Monday that he reached out to Miami Heat forward Giannis Antetokounmpo to apologize for a remark he made on a recent podcast.

Rivers, now an NBC Sports NBA analyst, coached Rivers in Milwaukee for parts of three seasons before being relieved of his duties at the end of last season. Rivers told "The Bill Simmons Podcast" in an episode posted last Thursday that Antetokounmpo "doesn't necessarily have this super IQ" for basketball and that he "really has one way: downhill, force, force."

Rivers told ESPN Andscape he meant to say "feel for the game" instead of "super IQ," he felt bad about the error in words and texted Antetokounmpo an apology that the latter responded positively to.

"I was saying he was one of the most interesting guys," Rivers said. "He makes unbelievable passes, but at then at times because of his force he plays at it gets in the way of his feel. It was more of a compliment. I hate this and feel bad about it. I apologize for the distraction. I'm not trying to be one."

Rivers also said Antetokounmpo was "not easy" to coach during the podcast. The Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame coach told Andscape that those comment were actually meant as a compliment to his greatness, not as a slight. Rivers also added that he made a lot of positive comments on the podcast about Antetokounmpo, including enjoying coaching the former Bucks star, that were overlooked.

"The point was trying to make is whenever you have a great player, you have to fit the team around that great player," Rivers told ESPN Andscape. "That is the point I was trying to make. It's not always easy. It's a compliment. I've been successful and unsuccessful at it. But your job is to create the best team you can possibly create around that great player and his talents."

Antetokounmpo addressed Rivers' comments Sunday, three days after the interview was published.

"First of all, he's not my coach," Antetokounmpo told reporters after Miami's 114-108 victory over the Sacramento Kings. "My coach is Coach Spo [Erik Spoelstra], but [Rivers] is a guy -- a coach -- that I've worked with in the past. I'm speechless."

Antetokounmpo, 31, is averaging 27.5 points and 12.8 rebounds in his first season with the Heat, who have rebounded from a slow start and improved to 4-6 with Sunday's victory in Sacramento.

stories.headline: Dianna Russini returning to sports media with show, column for BetUS
stories.summary: Dianna Russini is returning to sports media with a new weekly football show and column for the Costa Rica-based gambling company BetUS.
stories.body:
Dianna Russini is returning to sports media.

Russini, the former Athletic and ESPN NFL reporter, will launch a new weekly football show, and write a column with her league insights for the Costa Rica-based gambling company BetUS.

Russini's BetUS show will debut Wednesday, marking her first media venture since April, when she resigned from The Athletic after the New York Post published photographs showing her and New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel hugging and holding hands at an adults-only Arizona resort.

The Athletic published a report over the summer that found Russini violated company policy by not disclosing her relationship with Vrabel, but that it had little effect on her coverage.

Russini told People Magazine on Monday that navigating the media firestorm after the photos were first published was difficult but that the NFL community of players and executives was a source of support.

"The absolute best part of this situation has been the loyalty the NFL has shown me," Russini said.

She said players checked on her often and encouraged her to return to covering the league, adding, "They became sort of the people that I was learning from during this."

Her new show, The Russini Report, will include gambling analysis and weekly game previews, including commentary from NFL experts. Super Bowl champion coach Bill Parcells and sports radio personality Damon Amendolara will be Russini's first guests.

BetUS streams content on its website and on the social media platform X.

Russini will also appear on the podcast of sports media personality Jon Weiner, better known as Stugotz, to deliver NFL analysis.

Before the Athletic, Russini worked as an NFL reporter for ESPN.

stories.headline: Jets disappointed ex-goalie Connor Hellebuyck sitting out
stories.summary: The Jets are disappointed they won't get closure for the departure of ex-goalie Connor Hellebuyck as he won't be starting for the Devils when they play in Winnipeg on Tuesday.
stories.body:
The Winnipeg Jets wanted closure on Connor Hellebuyck and feel the New Jersey Devils are refusing to give it to them.

Hellebuyck was expected to get the start in Winnipeg on Tuesday night, facing the Jets for the first time since his trade demand was granted Oct. 23, when he waived his no-movement clause to join the Devils. But after Hellebuyck's 4-0 shutout win over the Toronto Maple Leafs on Sunday, Devils general manager Sunny Mehta announced an "organizational decision" that Hellebuyck would not start Tuesday night.

"Connor Hellebuyck was adamant that he felt a duty to play on Tuesday in Winnipeg. However, in our estimation, playing in this game would potentially give us a reduction in our expected win probability," he said in a news release, adding that Hellebuyck will meet the media in Winnipeg on Tuesday.

A one-time NHL MVP and three-time Vezina Trophy winner, Hellebuyck was suspended by the Jets after failing to report to training camp following his trade request. He played 11 seasons in Winnipeg.

Jets coach Scott Arniel on Monday expressed his disappointment in the Devils' decision -- and its justification.

"I've seen a lot of analytics in my life. I'm not sure how this works into the analytics part of it," he said. "I know it's their decision. They can do whatever they want. But that would put closure to it. This doesn't."

Devils coach Sheldon Keefe said that the plan was for Hellebuyck to play both games in a home-and-home series against the division rival Washington Capitals after the Winnipeg game, while citing the fact that Hellebuyck missed all of training camp and nearly the first month of the season.

But even with that explanation, Jets players were stunned Hellebuyck wasn't getting the net against them.

"To be honest, I didn't even think that was a possibility. I thought he was playing for sure," said winger Kyle Connor, who won a gold medal with Hellebuyck on Team USA at the 2026 Winter Olympics. "I think we all hoped that he was playing."

Jets captain Adam Lowry, who, like Connor, was a longtime teammate of Hellebuyck's, said there was disappointment among Winnipeg players about the decision, as the Devils are expected to start Jake Allen on Tuesday.

"I would have loved to play against him. We'd all be lying if we said we weren't looking forward to the opportunity," Lowry said. "He's a good friend of ours. It's always fun to go up against buddies or ex-teammates. You always want to best them. The atmosphere would have been great. It would have been an emotional night and a lot of fun."

While the fans are still expected to bring the venom for Hellebuyck despite him not playing -- as NHL fans have already seen this season when Brady Tkachuk returned to Ottawa and Quinn Hughes returned to Vancouver after contentious exits -- Lowry said the players aren't lamenting that lack of catharsis.

"From a player's standpoint, I don't feel like I've been robbed of anything. Obviously, there was a big buildup for the fans to either thank him or voice their displeasure, whatever that may be. They'll just have to wait a little longer," he said.

But Arniel wasn't happy that the Hellebuyck drama will stretch beyond Tuesday night.

"To me, it goes back to the ownership and the fans and the core players that have been with Helly since the very beginning, [the ones] that he left on," he said. "That's the part for me that's hard. He gave up on us. It would be nice to finally be done with this. All this does is drag this out and [make us] talk about it again,"

The Jets visit New Jersey on Saturday, Nov. 28. Hellebuyck is 5-0-0 since joining the Devils, with a 1.96 goals-against average and a .913 save percentage.

"I can feel the frustration of the fans. We wanted to put this thing to bed, and it's going to linger here," Arniel said. "We just wanted to get this game over and done with and let the fans react how they're going to react. I don't care about his opinion on things. I just wanted this to end."

stories.headline: CF Montréal owner Joey Saputo announces club is up for sale
stories.summary: CF Montréal owner Joey Saputo announced Monday that he has initiated the sale of the MLS club his family founded in 1992.
stories.body:
CF Montréal owner Joey Saputo announced he will initiate the process of sale for the Major League Soccer club.

"After more than three decades of commitment, we believe this is the appropriate time to begin the process of identifying new ownership for CF Montréal," Saputo said on Monday. "This club has been a central part of our lives."

The Saputo family first founded the Montreal Impact in 1992 before the club became the Canadian MLS team CF Montréal in 2012.

"We have dedicated significant time, energy and resources to building it, and we are proud of what CF Montréal has become. I would also like to thank the fans, whose passion and loyalty have been at the heart of this club," Saputo said.

"We believe this is the right time to welcome a new ownership group with the resources, vision and commitment to build on the strong foundation we have established and carry forward the club's proud legacy."

Montréal concluded the 2026 regular season in last place of the Eastern Conference table with 26 points and just six wins in 34 games. The team fired head coach Marco Donadel in April after a slow start to the season, letting go of Montreal's 11th manager in 14 seasons.

Saputo confirmed the team will continue to be operational until a sale is confirmed.

Saputo added he prefers the team be sold to a local buyer, but cannot control if the team relocates to another market.

"If the club doesn't find a local buyer and I get an offer where the club needs to be relocated, then I have no choice. That is the decision I will take," he said. "Our clear preference is to find a buyer who shares our commitment to Montréal and who will ensure the club remains in the city."

The Saputo family has retained BMO Capital Markets as lead financial advisor and National Bank Financial as co-advisor to manage the sale process and identify potential buyers.

The club announced that day-to-day operations will continue as usual throughout the selling period.

stories.headline: From an ACL tear to a time trial PB: Koby LeCras on building resilience in his draft year
stories.summary: Rangy wing-forward Koby LeCras saw a breakout year derailed by a partially torn ACL, but six weeks back running was enough to deliver a personal-best 2km time. He talks to Jasper Chellappah about his recovery and future ahead of the 2026 AFL Draft.
stories.body:
Koby LeCras wasn't expected to test at the AFL Draft combine. He also wasn't expected to be named best afield amongst the premier prospects of the 2026 draft class, or make his senior WAFL debut in his dad's No. 20 for West Perth.

It was a blazing start to his season that put the nephew of former West Coast forward Mark firmly in first-round contention. From there it all unravelled.

LeCras suffered a partially torn ACL in that WAFL debut. Senior football, the national championships, and flag tilts were all wiped away. It was a cruel end to a year that promised so much.

But the teenager was desperate to get back for something on his calendar, and the final destination for all draft hopefuls is the combine.

Despite just six weeks of training post-injury, LeCras turned out for the 2km time trial. He ran a 6:23, good for a top-15 time and a personal best under heavy duress.

"Going into it I had 6:25 written on my hand, so I got away with a couple seconds," LeCras told ESPN.

"When I started running it was the goal to do the 2km and the 20m sprint at the combine. I knew what the plan was, where I was going to be and what I was going to do."

Worries had been lurking at the back of Lecras's mind. He avoided surgery on the partial tear but it was difficult for him to regain 100% confidence in his knee when he got back to running.

"You look at Gryan Miers, you can rush it back. Being your draft year and you've obviously got a lot more footy to play than just this year [West Perth] were pretty quick to shut that down, that I wasn't going to play again.

"I just wanted to get back as quick as I could, whether it was combine or day one of pre-season. They said 'Yeah you can do the combine and then definitely back for day one of pre-season'."

LeCras's injury was devastating timing given the showing he'd treated recruiters to the previous week. Off a wing, the 192cm utility was best afield for the AFL Academy - a representative side featuring the best of the draft class thrown together against VFL opposition.

LeCras kicked three goals from 19 disposals and nine marks, commanding the air and showing off that aerobic endurance in defence and attack.

It was a performance reminiscent of Ollie Dempsey's ability to capitalise on mismatches with his strong hands in marking contests and sniff out opportunities in dangerous areas.

LeCras was delivering on the next evolution of the winger in the AFL, but he was playing up the ground out of team need and still sees himself as a forward 50 threat.

"I think I'm a natural forward, but I'm open to playing anywhere, whether it's halfback, wing, hopefully inside one day maybe.

"I love watching specific players, I'm probably a bit of a nuff.

"I love watching Jeremy Cameron, I reckon he's a superstar. And then obviously Logan Morris as well, sort of that undersized key forward. I love what he does and how he finds ways to beat his defenders. He's a freak, he's next level."

Koby's uncle Mark LeCras is one of the more underrated small forwards to play in the modern era. The one club player booted 441 goals from 219 games, and was the oldest player in the Eagles's 2018 triumph before retiring.

Similarly to his uncle, Koby is adept at twisting onto his preferred left foot and finding the goals from uncanny positions. He possesses natural forward craft, from leading patterns at challenging size to match up on to a natural, repeatable set shot action and goal nous from tight angles.

While his dad Brent enjoyed his own 141-game WAFL career, Koby's uncle continues to be a wealth of information as he prepares to step up to the AFL level.

"He's been massive. In the pre-season I watched a lot of vision with him, little ways to improve my game," LeCras said.

"If I could be half the player he was, I'd be really happy with that."

Mark's best day came against Essendon in 2010 at Etihad Stadium, kicking 12 goals straight. He booted 46 goals from 15 games against the Bombers in his career.

"We always joke about that, if he played against Essendon every week he would've kicked a thousand. That's what he reckons!"

stories.headline: MLB free agency tracker: 2026-27 offseason trades, moves
stories.summary: We've got you covered on all the major MLB hot stove signings and trades.
stories.body:
The 2026-27 MLB hot stove was lit just days after the Milwaukee Brewers hoisted the franchise's first World Series championship trophy.

All eyes this winter are on the free agency of two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. But he's not the only one who will make a splash in the market, with Freddy Peralta, Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki and Michael King among the other free agents to watch.

Which teams will go big to contend for the 2027 World Series title? And who will make the trades and signings that have everyone buzzing?

Below is a running list of notable transactions and updates from throughout the MLB offseason.

More: Best fits for top free agents | Latest on Skubal

Notable offseason transactions

Nov. 6

Mets re-sign pitcher Robert Stock to one-year contract.

Nov. 2

New York Yankees closer David Bednar, Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki and Seattle outfielder Randy Arozarena were among eight players who received $23.15 million qualifying offers from their teams Monday.

Sources: Chicago Cubs decline $7.5 million option for pitcher Colin Rea.

Nov. 1

San Diego Padres decline options on Nick Pivetta, Lucas Giolito, Griffin Canning; exercise option on Hart.

Garrett Whitlock's $8.25 million option exercised by Boston Red Sox.

Oct. 31

Tampa Bay Rays pick up $20 million option on ace pitcher Drew Rasmussen.

Oct. 29

Atlanta Braves exercise options on Ronald Acuña Jr., Ozzie Albies.

Seattle Mariners exercise Andrés Muñoz option, decline Victor Robles, Bryce Miller option.

Key offseason dates

Oct. 29: Players become free agents, trades open for players on 40-man rosters

Nov. 2: Deadline to exercise contract options, extend qualifying offers

Nov. 2 (5 p.m. ET): MLB free agents can begin signing with other teams

Nov. 10-12: MLB general manager meetings

Nov. 17-19: MLB owners meetings

Nov. 20: Non-tender deadline

Dec. 1: Current MLB collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET

stories.headline: 'The World Cup never really ended': U.S.-based betting sees rise in wagering on MLS, European soccer
stories.summary: Before the World Cup, many wondered if Americans would stick around afterward. Betting data says yes, they did.
stories.body:
Soccer was the sport of the summer in the United States this year, as the FIFA World Cup came to 11 American cities (in addition to venues in Canada and Mexico). Americans embraced the sport fully, supporting tremendous numbers for television viewership and stadium attendance -- as well as sports betting handle.

BetMGM said that the World Cup "nearly kept pace with the MLB's rigorous summer schedule" despite there being five times as many baseball games over that time period. Hard Rock Bet noted the tournament did three times as much handle and brought in double the number of individual bettors as the men's NCAA tournament, which is traditionally the most-bet-on event on the U.S. sports calendar.

In Colorado, which breaks down betting revenue by sport, the World Cup generated $60.2 million, a near 250% increase from the $17.5 million brought in by the previous edition of the tournament in November 2022.

With European league soccer in full swing and Major League Soccer kicking off playoffs, that momentum has continued over for the American sports betting ecosystem.

BetMGM noted that in the two-month period immediately following the conclusion of the 2026 World Cup, the sportsbook saw a 24.5% year-over-year increase in bets and a 34.5% increase in handle on wagers for club soccer. Hard Rock said there have been nearly 30% more wagers on soccer overall, specifically 43% more in the Premier League and 21% in the Champions League with World Cup stars Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland and Harry Kane attracting double the amount of bets in the competition compared to the same time period last year.

"The World Cup never really ended for our customers. The bettors who did well backing Mbappé, Haaland and Kane this summer have followed them straight back to the Champions League, and the post-World Cup pain continues for us every time those guys light up the scoreboard," Hard Rock Bet SVP of sportsbook Neil Walsh told ESPN over email. "Those Tuesday and Wednesday afternoon matches don't compete with primetime U.S. sports, so they get our customers' full attention."

"We have seen an immediate increase in activity across our soccer markets when comparing 2026 with 2025," Caesars lead soccer trader Mark Bickerdike said in an email.

"Encouragingly, that growth is evident across both pre-match and in-play betting and is reflected across the majority of competitions we offer. It certainly feels as though we've benefited from the momentum generated by the World Cup heading into the new domestic seasons."

MLS has attracted significantly more betting action in 2026 than it did the year before, showing a 30.4% increase in tickets and a 38.8% increase in money from mid-July to the end of October. MLS handle is up 27% at Hard Rock Bet over a similar time period, with Inter Miami -- a fixture for the Florida-based book -- garnering almost 40% more bets year-over-year.

"We've seen a jump up in more users that are betting soccer and a lot of that is from MLS," DraftKings director of sports operations Johnny Avello told ESPN. "We'd like to think that's from people betting the World Cup this year and finding out that soccer's a fun game to wager on."

The development of MLS' betting market comes in the wake of unprecedented popularity for the league and as it looks to transition to a fall-spring schedule that lines up with the rest of world soccer.

Bickerdike said that since Aug. 1, MLS has moved from being Caesars' fourth-most bet soccer league to second. The revised calendar could benefit the league further.

"It creates the opportunity for customers to engage with a full day of soccer, starting with competitions such as the Premier League and LaLiga before moving into a slate of MLS fixtures later in the day," said Bickerdike. "From a sportsbook perspective, our market offering is consistent across these competitions, creating a seamless experience for customers and potentially encouraging greater engagement with MLS over time."

Coming out of MLS Decision Day on Saturday, Nashville SC are the favorites for the MLS Cup at +400. Thomas Müller's Vancouver Whitecaps and Lionel Messi's Inter Miami (the reigning champions) follow just behind at +450.

stories.headline: Toto Wolff: Mercedes face fierce 2027 battle after winning constructors' title
stories.summary: Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has played down the suggestion his team is about to embark on another period of dominance in Formula 1, and believes the battle for the 2027 title has already started.
stories.body:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has played down the suggestion his team is about to embark on another period of dominance in Formula 1, and believes the battle for the 2027 title has already started.

They sealed the constructors' championship with three races of the season remaining at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday, just one week after Kimi Antonelli secured the drivers' championship in Mexico City.

The German manufacturer stole a march on its rivals at the start of the year following the introduction of new engine regulations and has continued to be competitive throughout the season.

But after winning just one race in the last five, Wolff believes rival teams Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari are in a position to pose a serious threat for the title in 2027.

"Look at the last few races, we haven't won," Wolff said. "And today at the beginning of the race, Kimi was just storming away, it looked like this could be ours, but the competition has been getting tougher, between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves.

"It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year.

"So for me, the 2027 season has started now. It is about learning in the three last races.

"What is it we can optimise? What didn't we spot when we put the upgrade on the car? What is it we can learn from today, and attack these last three races full blast, whilst also making sure that we have the learning for next year's power unit and next year's car."

Wolff believes the sheer quality of the top teams on the grid means the era of runaway teams in new regulations cycles -- such as Mercedes from 2014 and Red Bull from 2022 -- is a thing of the past.

"It looks like the most competitive era that is about to start, because the teams have become so professional in capability, in resource, that these kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them anymore, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row," he said. "And that is a completely new challenge.

"You can see how quickly it goes from being dominant and within a few races you realise that your upgrade doesn't work and you fall back and you're just third on the road. So it's great for the sport.

"I wish it was the era of Mercedes and me running away with another few titles, but I don't think it's the reality."

- Wet weather mastery by Norris, Verstappen makes Brazil F1's must-see race

- Mercedes completes the double with constructors' title at São Paulo Grand Prix

Wolff believes one of the keys to Mercedes' success remains its no-blame culture and its ability to empower its employees.

"We have stability certainly as a factor, but we have also many people that have joined us recently, and I think what I would like to choose as a word is safety. We are not a high-and-fire organisation.

"We provide a culture and an environment where you can thrive, where you are allowed to make mistakes, where you can speak up. And over the long term, I believe, if you want to be successful, not over a period of a few years, but over many decades, this is what you need to be able to kind of ingrain in the team. And we're trying that.

"It's not something you put on a PowerPoint. You have to live those standards in and out. These are the standards we are setting for ourselves.

"Sometimes we fail, but we look at the long-term vision. For me, soon is in ten years, and I need to set the team up for soon."

stories.headline: Conor McGregor insists it has to be Max Holloway for final UFC fight
stories.summary: Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.
stories.body:
Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.

Back in July, Holloway (28-9) defeated McGregor (22-7) via TKO in just 69 seconds, after McGregor injured his right knee in the opening seconds of their welterweight bout in Las Vegas.

Speaking at the BKFC Glasgow post-fight news conference on Saturday, McGregor, 38, once again reiterated his desire to run it back with Holloway.

"It has to be Holloway," McGregor told reporters.

"Just do the f------ thing again. Just do the thing again. The guy didn't engage once. He's the one that called for the stoppage in the fight. He said 'ref, ref!'

"He's the one stopping the fight. Imagine I just said 'yay!' and jumped the fence. I won! He doesn't want to f------ fight.

"On the one leg, he wasn't coming near me. It's so shocking and so heartbreaking to me and I'm still f------ dealing with it. It has to be Holloway. Just f------ dust it off, re-do it."

On the rehab, McGregor stated he's looking for a return potentially before the summer next year and also hinted if Holloway isn't available he could look elsewhere for an opponent.

"I'm on my way back," McGregor said.

"What's it now November? Three months I'm off of surgery. I done this injury before and returned within nine months. So nine months is pre-summer. I just want to go again and again."

"Something might happen, I don't know. But a fighter that fights me, put some respect on my name. If you're not a world champion fighter, if you've not got world accolades to your name, don't utter my f------ name."

The fight against Holloway at UFC 329 was McGregor's first appearance since July 2021 and he has now suffered serious lower-body injuries in each of past two fights, including a fractured leg against Dustin Poirier in 2021.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: Eels recruit to miss NRL opener after ref gesture
stories.summary: Parramatta's marquee offseason recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign -- including the Eels trip to Las Vegas -- after being sinbinned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.
stories.body:
Parramatta's marquee offseason recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign -- including the Eels trip to Las Vegas -- after being sinbinned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.

Leniu was sinbinned by referee Adam Gee for dissent late in the first half of Sunday's 44-12 loss to the Kangaroos in Sydney.

The prop made a money gesture with his hand as he walked towards the tunnel, a sign that many interpreted as the Samoan forward questioning the integrity and impartiality of match officials.

Leniu was handed a grade three contrary conduct charge on Monday.

The 26-year-old, who will join Parramatta after winning the 2026 premiership with Sydney Roosters, will miss the club's opening two games of the season, which includes their trip to the US to face Gold Coast.

In the unlikely event he contests the charge, Leniu would incur an additional one-game ban if he were to lose his appeal.

The prop's outburst came during a frustrating night for Samoa, from which Samoan halves Ronald Volkman and Jarome Luai have avoided suspension for dangerous contact.

Samoa were on the wrong end of a 9-4 penalty count and coach Ben Gardiner suggested Gee had handed the Kangaroos several "home ground calls".

"It was a real home ground advantage for Australia," Gardiner said.

"They had the the music pumping in the background and we had a lot of Samoan fans here to support us, which was brilliant.

"But they got the home ground calls, got a really good start and then it was just too hard for us to chase back from there."

Brisbane winger Josiah Karapani will also be a late starter next season after he was hit with a two-game suspension by the NRL following a drink driving charge in June.

Karapani, one of Brisbane's best last season, also received an infringement notice for speeding, along with further penalties for failure to display P plates and driving an unregistered and uninsured vehicle.

In court, he was fined $350 and disqualified from driving for three months.

He had already served a club-imposed one-game suspension last season, with the NRL on Monday adding a $1500 suspended fine and obligation to complete an education and training session.

It was his second off-field indiscretion in the season after he was previously stood down by the Broncos for a public nuisance offence in March.

stories.summary: Andre Snellings breaks down Monday's eight-game NBA slate, highlighting the fantasy streamers to add and bets to make.
stories.body:
ESPN's basketball daily cheat sheet is your pregame destination before you lock in daily fantasy and betting decisions for that night's games. Here you'll find our top insights for the slate, including players to target for your daily fantasy rosters, along with game-by-game injury reports.

What you need to know for Monday
The NBA starts off this week with eight games on the docket, including three between two teams that both enter with winning records.

The first such matchup features the red-hot Los Angeles Lakers traveling to Atlanta to face the Hawks. The Lakers defeated the Detroit Pistons on Sunday even with Luka Doncic (back) sidelined, behind 43 points from Austin Reaves. Doncic is questionable to return for tonight's game.

The Memphis Grizzlies (6-3) head north of the border to face the Toronto Raptors (5-4). Memphis' Ty Jerome has scored more than 20 points in three straight games, his second such streak of the season, and will try to get to a fourth tonight.

And in Houston, two early-season MVP candidates lock horns when the Rockets (7-3) host the Denver Nuggets (5-3). The key to tonight's win might be which of Nikola Jokic and Kevin Durant are able to put on a more MVP-caliber performance.

With an eye toward uncovering compelling betting angles and potential fantasy streamers, let's take a closer look at all of tonight's action.

Fantasy stream team
Players available in at least 50% of leagues

Jakob Poeltl, C, Toronto Raptors (rostered in 36.3% of ESPN basketball leagues)
Poeltl has been dealing with a shoulder injury that slowed his start to the season, but he had a breakout in his last outing that suggested he is on the road to recovery. On Friday, with Scottie Barnes (groin) sidelined, Poeltl dropped 19 points, 11 boards and 3 steals in 31 minutes. This marked his second double-double in his last three games played.

Saddiq Bey, SF/PF, New Orleans Pelicans (35.9%)
Bey is fully settled into his role as the shooting/scoring sixth man for the Pelicans. Even though he comes off the bench, in many games Bey becomes one of the primary scorer on the team when he is locked in. He often finishes halves, which keeps him playing near starter-minutes. In his last five games, Bey has averaged 19.8 PPG, 1.8 3PG and 1.4 SPG in 29.6 MPG.

P.J. Washington, PF/SF, Dallas Mavericks (36.8%)
Washington has started every game this season, notching double digits in either points or rebounds, or both, in nine of 10 games. He has scored 20 or more points in two of his last three games, including a 21-point/10-rebound game that marked his second 20-10 effort of the season.

Quenton Jackson, PG/SG, Indiana Pacers (5.0%)
Jackson has stepped into a larger role with Tyrese Haliburton sidelined. He still comes off the bench for the Pacers, but has moved up into a sixth man role with the occasional spot start. In his last five games, four as a reserve and one as a starter, Jackson has averaged 15.0 PPG, 1.8 3PG and 1.6 SPG in 24.2 MPG.

Dre's bets to make on Monday
Odds by DraftKings and subject to change.

Austin Reaves OVER 22.5 points (-110)
This is an interesting line for Reaves. On the one hand, Doncic will play tonight after missing last night's game. Reaves dropped 43 on the Pistons yesterday with Doncic out. But even in games with Doncic, Reaves has scored more than 23 points in six of nine contests. It's a reasonable line for him.

Editor's Note: Reaves is listed as questionable (illness) for this game.

Ty Jerome OVER 21.5 points (-116)
Jerome enters this game averaging 26.6 PPG, having scored 21 or more in three straight and six of his eight games so far. Jerome dealt with back issues late in October that caused him to miss a game right after his two lowest scoring games of the season, but otherwise has been instant offense all season. He dropped 21 points in his last outing against the Oklahoma City Thunder, the team that has allowed by-far the fewest points to opposing point guards (18.6 PPG) in the NBA this season. Tonight, he'll face a friendlier Raptors defense that is middle of the pack (25.6 PPG allowed to opposing point guards, 15th in NBA) in points allowed to his position.

Dallas Mavericks -3.5 OVER Indiana Pacers (-112)
The Mavericks (6-4) are off to a solid start, and have won two straight games. The Pacers (3-7) are struggling, with losses in six of their last seven games. The most recent five of those losses were all by more than 3.5 points. With Tyrese Haliburton sidelined, the Pacers don't have the same ceiling. Playing at home, with their relative levels of play, the Mavericks should be favored to win this game by a solid margin.

stories.headline: Sporting KC fires Raphael Wicky after last-place finish in West
stories.summary: Sporting Kansas City fired coach Raphael Wicky after one season on Monday, which means the MLS club will have its fourth coach since March 2025 when it begins the league's sprint season in February.
stories.body:
KANSAS CITY, Kan. -- Sporting Kansas City fired coach Raphael Wicky after one season on Monday, which means the MLS club will have its fourth coach since March 2025 when it begins the league's sprint season in February.

Sporting KC finished the season with a 1-0 win over San Diego on Saturday, leaving the club just 7-23-5 across all competitions and last in the Western Conference. The 26 points were the second-fewest in the history of the club.

Wicky replaced longtime coach Peter Vermes and his replacement, Kerry Zavagnin, who became the interim coach when Vermes and the club parted early last year. Wicky previously coached Young Boys in his native Switzerland and Chicago Fire FC in MLS.

"We would like to thank Raphael for his time at Sporting KC," said David Lee, the club's president of soccer operations. "The season has been challenging for many reasons, and we recognize that Rapha and his staff worked incredibly hard in difficult circumstances. After a review of the season, Rapha and I met, and I decided to make the change. We wish Rapha the best of luck in the future."

State of play and players to know
Essendon will be on the clock first, holding the top selection a decade on from the last time it took the number one pick to the AFL Draft. The Dons are expected to first bid on Port Adelaide-tied forward Dougie Cochrane, which will trigger a start-of-second-round compensation pick for the Bombers, Tigers and Eagles.

There are familial lines drawn throughout an exciting 2008-born cohort. Cody Walker is the son of high-flying Blue Andrew and will be headed to Princes Park. Cochrane is the son of former North Melbourne and Port Adelaide midfielder Stuart, though he isn't eligible to either team under the 100-game father-son rule. Instead, he's eligible to join the Power as part of their Next Generation Academy as an Indigenous prospect.

Top-10 riser Sam Gayfer is the nephew of 1990 premiership Pie Mick, and Koby LeCras brings goalkicking pedigree via 2018 premiership uncle Mark.

There will be up to five club-tied talents picked in the first round of the AFL Draft. But that won't necessarily result in an extended first night. Over the past five years the first round has averaged out to 25 selections accounting for father-son and academy bids, but clubs are expecting a number closer to the traditional 18 picks in the final intake of the 18-team competition.

Stricter stipulations around matching bids is at play, with clubs only able to use a maximum of two selections when matching for a club-tied prospect, meaning the selections of Port Adelaide, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS will be absorbed as early bids are matched.

We could see a record number of Indigenous talents picked in the first round. The high-water mark was four in 2005 and 2014, and all of Cochrane, Walker, Caylen Murray (Lions Academy), Toby Krasna and Jake Eime could be taken in the first round in 2026.

Thirteen of the top prospects have already been invited to Marvel Stadium on November 19.

Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody are all still in contention to be the open pool No. 1 pick, with Harry Van Hattum, Gus Teixeira, Mitch Harris and Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) rounding out the group on top of draft boards alongside Cochrane and Walker.

Murray, Gayfer, Wil Malady and Leo Steed have also received invites in a sign of club interest on night one.

Around 65 picks are expected to be taken across both nights which would surpass the 60 selections last year.

stories.headline: What if Manchester United had hired Jurgen Klopp?
stories.summary: If Manchester United hired an all-time great like Jurgen Klopp, would they have won the Premier League? Let's find out!
stories.body:
Right around this time every year, you can start to feel it. The air gets a little crisper. The shadows get a little colder. The days get shorter. The tree colors start to pop. You start wearing sweaters. Pumpkins appear in places where they do and do not belong.

Everyone and everything starts to shift, just slightly, in preparation for what's about to happen. The cycles of nature can be fickle and unpredictable, so the date is never exactly the same, and some years come and go without anything at all. But most years, it does.

Our tiny little rituals prime us to anticipate the inevitable, oncoming shift: that moment when Manchester United fire their manager and convince themselves that the new guy is finally going to be the one who fixes everything.

Ruben Amorim lost his job last January. Erik ten Hag was fired two years ago, right before Halloween. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer got the boot just a couple of days before Thanksgiving. And Jose Mourinho was relieved of his duties a little over a week before Christmas.

Now that we've once again entered the season of sacking, Michael Carrick seems like he will inevitably become the latest victim.

Man United are in the relegation zone. If history is any indication, their comeback against AS Roma in the Champions League will end up being meaningless. Before Tuesday's win, Carrick appeared to be on the verge of tears at the end of every match.

This is the 14th season since Manchester United last won the Premier League. And whoever replaces Carrick will be the ninth coach to try to do something that no other United manager since has done: just, simply, meet the expectations at one of the richest sports teams on the planet for more than a single season in a row.

But given how many different coaches have now failed since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club, it makes you wonder: Could anyone have been successful at Manchester United?

What is a great manager worth?

Arsenal won the Premier League last season with 85 points.

If we lived in a world where there were no subs and everyone on the field contributed exactly evenly to their team's success, then all 11 Arsenal players would have contributed about 8 points (7.7, to be slightly more exact) of value last season.

Except, the alternative to each player isn't just zero points. If you removed Bukayo Saka from the lineup, you wouldn't have to play a man down. No, you'd get to put another player out there who would also contribute to winning to some degree.

So, let's look at the relegation-level cutoff. West Ham were relegated with 39 points. Using the same framework, we'd say that all of their players were worth a little over 3.5 points across the season. We could then say that the average Arsenal player provided 5 more points of value than a relegation-level player.

This, of course, isn't exactly how it works: Some players are better than others, some positions are more valuable than others, and almost nobody plays 100% of the minutes. Goalkeeper David Raya played 97.3% of the league minutes last season, and Declan Rice led all outfield Gunners with 90.5% of minutes played.

But it all still gives us a nice benchmark. The best players on the best teams in the world are probably worth around 7 points more than your average relegation-level player. The truly generational superstars? You could probably bump that number up to 10 points if you wanted to.

But what about the manager? Rather than litigating the whole "managers don't matter" conversation for the 1,000th time on this website, we're just going to go with the logic put forth by Liverpool's former director of research, Ian Graham, in his book, "How to Win the Premier League": "[About] the same value as a good player brings. This is in line with manager salaries -- the best managers are paid a similar wage to the best players."

Who, then, was the best manager that Manchester United could've hired at any point over the past 14 seasons?

Most soccer-watchers would agree that there are two potential answers: Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. And most analyses would agree.

A 2025 study from the Sloan Sports Analytics conference looked at team performances from 2017 through 2024 across Europe's Big Five top leagues. The study awarded or penalized the manager for how much a team's performance level exceeded or undershot expectations based on the talent of the roster. Klopp and Guardiola topped the list -- with a significant gap between themselves and the next tier of coaches.

Given the 114 guilty charges against Manchester City under Guardiola, though, I think we have to go with Klopp. While Guardiola's influence on how the sport is played is undeniable, we now have to look on his Man City tenure skeptically. We know how much they outperformed what we were told they spent, but it would be foolish to blindly accept those numbers and attribute the gap purely to the Guardiola effect.

With Klopp, though, we know that he turned two clubs that were not even the richest clubs in their own leagues into two of the best teams in the world. And we know that he maintained those levels -- at both clubs -- for many seasons in a row. On top of that, both Borussia Dortmund and now Liverpool seem to have gotten worse after he left each job.

The job of the manager, simply, is to make his team better than the talent his club can afford to acquire and then to keep that improvement going even as the roster turns over. At the highest level of the sport, Klopp was better at that than any of his peers.

Could the best manager in the world save Manchester United?

What, then, might've happened if Manchester United somehow managed to hire Jurgen Klopp back in 2013 instead of David Moyes?

There are, of course, all kinds of ripple effects we could tease out -- what it would've done to German soccer, where Liverpool would've ended up, how Mohamed Salah's career would've played out, and on and on.

But I just want to focus on what it would've meant for Manchester United. We know that Liverpool benefitted from hiring Jurgen Klopp. But we also know that Jurgen Klopp benefitted from working for a club that did things like convincing him to sign Mohamed Salah instead of Julian Brandt.

Liverpool's cutting-edge front office didn't turn the club into the best team in the world, and neither did Klopp. No, it was the combo of the two that did it.

We could say similarly about Borussia Dortmund. At the time, Dortmund were one of the leaders in both youth development and identifying young stars. This meant that Klopp got the ideal kinds of talent, energetic youngsters to play his high-pressing style: Robert Lewandowski, Mats Hummels, Marco Reus, and Ilkay Gündogan -- just to name a few.

What we know about Manchester United, broadly, is that the club is an abject disaster. In terms of doing things that increase their chances of winning games, they are pretty much as bad as it gets. Since 2013, United have finished at or higher in the table than their relative Premier League revenue ranking once -- and that was last season.

While we could employ some magical thinking and convince ourselves that the only problem here is that the club can't hire the right coach, that's obviously not true. If it were, it would mean that the club that keeps firing its coaches just so happens to be doing all of the other things right.

No, the failure to find a successful long-term coach is a symptom of all of the other issues that plague the club. They've so badly underperformed their resources for over a decade; we can confidently say there is something deeply wrong with the way Manchester United tries to build its soccer teams.

So, if Klopp were the Man United coach, he wouldn't have fixed all of those problems. No, he would've had to work within that dysfunctional environment. He would've, in other words, ended up with Brandt instead of Salah -- many times over.

But let's sketch out the absolute best-case scenario for this hypothetical. Let's say that United have continued to hire "relegation-quality" managers. And let's say that Klopp's value is equivalent not just to the best player on a title team but to a true, once-in-a-generation superstar.

Neither of those things is true -- United aren't constantly hiring genuinely bad coaches, and Klopp himself would tell you that he's not worth the same as Lionel Messi -- but stretching the effect out to the extreme helps make the point.

Plus, by applying a Messi-like effect every year, we're canceling out some of the other problems with this exercise: not addressing the Manchester City situation, not subtracting points from other teams, not accounting for the increased spending power from an increased performance level, and so on.

If Klopp could've added 10 points to every Manchester United season, here's how things would've changed:

On average, United would've ended up with 76 points per season instead of 66, and their average finishing position would've been 3.8 instead of 5.3.

So, of course: things would be better if Manchester United had employed the best manager of the modern era for the last decade-plus. In this scenario, they would've finished in the top four 10 times, rather than six. Perhaps there would've been a deep Champions League run at a club that reached three finals in four seasons from 2008 to 2011 and hasn't been beyond the quarterfinals since.

But even if we granted Manchester United 13 straight seasons of consistent, transformative, incomparable, once-in-a-generation managerial performance, the team would still find itself right where it sits today: with no Premier League titles since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club.

stories.headline: Oscar Piastri splits from Mark Webber's management after eventful seven years
stories.summary: McLaren driver Oscar Piastri has split with the management team headed by ex-Formula 1 driver Mark Webber.
stories.body:
McLaren driver Oscar Piastri has split with the management team headed by ex-Formula 1 driver Mark Webber.

Webber and his partner Ann Neal had managed Piastri's career since 2019, helping him negotiate his route to F1 by leaving the Alpine junior team and signing with McLaren.

Webber, who started 217 grands prix in his own career, had already reduced his presence trackside this year and a statement indicated a mutual decision had been reached to part ways.

"Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close," Webber said.

"This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career."

Piastri thanked Webber for his involvement in his career to date.

"I'd like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years," he said. "Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career.

"I wish them all the best going forward."

- Verstappen's P21 to P2: Red Bull a 'disaster to drive' in São Paulo

- Norris labels São Paulo win McLaren's 'best race in terms of execution'

- Wet weather mastery by Norris, Verstappen makes Brazil F1's must-see race

Piastri came within 13 points of becoming world champion last year in a tense battle for the title with teammate Lando Norris and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Now in his fourth season in F1, Piastri made his debut with McLaren after Alpine left a contractual door open for him to leave its junior programme in 2023.

The dispute went to an employment tribunal in late 2022, which ruled in Mclaren's favour allowing Piastri to join the team as Daniel Ricciardo's replacement.

Piastri is currently seventh in the drivers' standings with two podiums this season.

stories.headline: How the Atlanta Dream turned their franchise around in just five years
stories.summary: Five years ago, the Dream were the second-worst team in the WNBA -- making their Finals run all the more remarkable.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Just five years ago, the idea of the Atlanta Dream competing for the WNBA championship trophy would have seemed as unlikely as a rebound landing untouched next to Angel Reese.

So finishing within one victory of a title, as the Dream did in the WNBA Finals last week, says a lot about just how far the franchise has come since 2021. Even without the 2026 championship, what the Dream did in revitalizing their franchise is a story that shouldn't be lost in Golden State's celebration. Five years ago, the Dream were a mess. Now, they're contenders. That's something other WNBA franchises can look to.

"It's remarkable, really," Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said.

Consider how far the franchise was from this in 2021.

That was the year the Dream moved to Gateway Center Arena -- the smallest venue in the WNBA at 3,500 seats -- because too much of their longtime larger home (State Farm Arena, capacity 17,608) was vacant during games. The Dream had three different coaches that year, one resigning just before the season began to take a college job. Chennedy Carter, their lottery-pick selection from 2020, was suspended in July and never returned. They finished in second-to-last place in the WNBA at 8-24.

The team's most notable moment came not on court, but in a viral video of two Dream players throwing punches by a food truck outside an Atlanta nightclub.

Those were the low points. But behind the scenes, two big moves in 2021 helped spark a turnaround: an ownership change, led by real estate investor Larry Gottesdiener, and a new general manager, Dan Padover.

Reese was then a college sophomore with huge goals for her future. But it wasn't until this April that she knew those plans would intersect with the Dream.

"When I play with joy and I'm surrounded by people that just genuinely make me happy, I think I'm at my best," Reese said. "The organization has poured into me. To be in my third year [in the WNBA], this is obviously the best situation I've ever been in."

And even as Reese and teammates Jordin Canada and Allisha Gray sat somberly in the Dream's postgame news conference after Game 7, the joyful sounds of Ballhalla's celebration audible, they looked dissatisfied but not devastated.

"They changed my life," Reese said of the Atlanta players and staff. "And I'm just so grateful for them."

A 2008 EXPANSION TEAM, the Dream's first title hopes were led by another Angel -- 2009 No. 1 pick Angel McCoughtry. She led the Dream to the Finals in 2010, 2011 and 2013, but they were swept each time.

The Dream then missed the playoffs six of the next nine years. They won a then-franchise record 23 games in 2018, but lost McCoughtry to a knee injury Aug. 7 and lost 3-2 in the semifinals.

Without McCoughtry in 2019, the Dream averaged just 4,270 fans for home games, necessitating the move from State Farm Arena. That relocation was delayed a year because of the COVID-19 pandemic, when the 2020 season was in a "bubble" in Bradenton, Florida. By then, McCoughtry had left in free agency for Las Vegas.

The Dream's leadership became a focus for all WNBA players in the bubble when co-owner Kelly Loeffler sent a letter to commissioner Cathy Engelbert opposing the league's decision to display "Black Lives Matter" logos on the courts in Bradenton. Loeffler wrote "we need less -- not more -- politics in sports."

Loeffler was involved in a political race at the time, seeking to hold her U.S. Senate seat. The divide mushroomed into WNBA players campaigning for her opponent, Raphael Warnock.

"Being on the outside of the Dream looking in then, during that time everybody was rallying around them," said guard Jordin Canada, then with the Seattle Storm, of the bubble activism against Loeffler's continued ownership. "We wanted what was best for them and the W as a whole, and to see that transition into a more positive direction."

The situation was untenable, and the franchise was sold in February 2021 to Gottesdiener's group, which included former WNBA player Renee Montgomery.

"I believed the WNBA was an extraordinary opportunity, not just to grow the game of basketball," Gottesdiener said, "but to demonstrate what's possible when you invest in women."

Padover, who joined the Dream in October 2021, had worked for the Las Vegas Aces for three years, helping build the team that would become a three-time champion. He went from a franchise a step from the top to one with nowhere to go but up.

Padover started his WNBA career as a video coordinator with the New York Liberty in 2012, and he has credited former coach and GM Bill Laimbeer for helping him develop into a team executive. He cites this key from Laimbeer.

"If you can get your organization organized and you can take care of the players, you can start to establish yourself as a place that is respected," Padover said. "Under previous ownership, I think we were disorganized, and we didn't really have an identity.

"When I got here the goal was, 'Let's turn Atlanta back into a franchise that's respected throughout the WNBA community, one piece at a time, and that will allow us to be able to build something.' We started with things like player housing, staffing, and medical and player development."

THE OTHER PIECE was putting the right players and coaches in the building. Padover, who has been named the league's executive of the year three times, put his trade wizardry to use. He dealt the Nos. 3 and 14 picks in the 2022 draft and a 2023 pick swap to Washington for the No. 1 pick in 2022 to select Rhyne Howard.

"It was a huge boost of confidence," Howard said. "Obviously, when you get drafted, that means the team wants you. But to do it in the way that they did -- trading up to get me like that -- put no doubt in my mind that I was a piece that they were looking for to start this new journey, to start this new outcome that we're having."

The 6-foot-2 guard was Rookie of the Year and has since been a four-time All-Star. She averaged 17.7 points in the regular season this year and 16.3 in the playoffs. Howard won't recall Game 7 fondly -- she was limited to six points on 3-of-14 shooting -- but she took noticeable steps forward as a player in 2026, especially on defense.

Padover also got the steal of the second round in 2022 with forward Naz Hillmon, who became a full-time starter this season and has played more WNBA games than anyone from that draft class.

Subsequent huge deals came for guards Gray (2023) and Canada (2024).

"One of the things that I definitely took from Bill was not to be skittish to give up things in trades," Padover said. "If you're doing it to get a great player, it's always worth it, and don't be afraid to do that."

One of Padover's biggest moves in 2025 was bringing in Smesko, who had spent most of his career as a college coach, including 17 years at Florida Gulf Coast.

"Obviously, there was a changing landscape in college basketball, and I was at the point where a new challenge was needed," Smesko said of his decision to move to the WNBA. "It was Atlanta, and I love the city. And I thought there was the makings of a core that could compete for a championship."

Atlanta went 30-14 last season but lost in the first round of the playoffs. Padover used a trade to acquire the last key component. On April 6, the Dream obtained Reese from the Chicago Sky for future draft picks. Reese had become disillusioned with the Sky's direction and voiced her concerns near the end of the 2025 season. She believed in the Dream's vision, just as the players obtained before her did.

"I feel like the organization has gotten to a point where players want to come play for Atlanta," Gray said. "To be able to get Angel just speaks volumes of how the organization is run and how it really cares for players. The city of Atlanta is great. Great culture. The games just feel like one big family cookout, and everybody's welcome."

Reese proved to be the final and most essential ingredient. Other than a five-game skid June 24-July 4, the Dream -- who also added veteran DeWanna Bonner late in the season -- stayed consistent, finishing 30-14 again. Reese had the best offensive year of her career, averaging 16.4 points, plus 12.1 rebounds.

"She's made me look good all season long," Howard said. "And I'm sure she's going to continue to do that for the rest of her time here. Shoutout to her for coming in and being bought in. She's handled every challenge that we've thrown at her with grace."

This year's Finals games in Atlanta didn't come without hurdles -- facility conflicts with State Farm Arena meant one Finals game had to be moved up a day and another had to be played at 12:30 p.m. ET on a Thursday. But even that early game was joyful and loud, a full house of fans skipping work and school to cheer on the Dream in a must-win Game 6.

Next year, the Dream moves back to State Farm Arena full time, playing all 25 regular-season home games there.

And as disappointed as the Dream were after losing Game 7, they also immediately expressed excitement about the 2027 season.

"Just because we didn't win today doesn't mean that we won't be champions in the future," Reese said.

Those words weren't just platitudes after a disappointing ending. Next year, with every starter already signed to return, the Dream could at last win that elusive title.

"I like our chemistry and just the sisterhood that we have as a team," said Gray, who played every Finals game despite sustaining an injury on her shooting hand in the semifinals. "We actually love each other and enjoy being around each other."

stories.headline: US to host World Cup games but no guarantees of a spot
stories.summary: The 2030 Rugby League World Cup will be a five-week tournament staged across different cities in the US and Pacific.
stories.body:
Rugby League World Cup games will be hosted in North America for the first time, but the US national team will not be automatically handed a qualification spot for the 2030 tournament.

As part of the lead-up to this weekend's men's and women's finals between Australia and New Zealand in Brisbane, the International Rugby League (IRL) made several announcements on Monday, including the location of the 2030 tournament, which will be spread across the US and the Pacific.

Using a Magic Round-style format, a round of fixtures will be hosted in alternative cities across five weekends that includes three group-stage games, a semi-final and final.

The men's tournament will expand from 10 to 12 teams, with the women's increasing from eight to 10, as US locations such as Hawaii, Utah and California - where there are large Pasifika diasporas - appear early contenders to host fixtures.

But the US - which last competed at the 2017 men's tournament - will be forced to qualify for the event because the NRL and the Australian Rugby League Commission will shoulder the risk associated with running the 2030 World Cup.

"The evidence is there for everyone to see how exceptional the NRL's capability is," Grant said in Sydney on Monday.

"They do this in Vegas, as an example, and they're entering into a period where they're taking a global round into the market, so they're the perfect partners for us.

"Their professionalism is unmatched in rugby league, and I've worked with Peter V'landys for 12 years now ... you've seen the impact he's had here in rugby league, so I've got nothing but confidence, as does my entire board."

Grant said the IRL had considered hosting the 2030 tournament in Europe as the NRL nears an investment deal in the Super League, but revealed it was his "aspiration" to host the 2034 tournament across Europe and North America.

As well as announcing the 2030 hosts, Grant revealed discussions were under way to raise Tonga and Samoa from tier-two to tier-one nations.

"We want to go through a consultation process to ensure that there's no unintended consequences from that decision, so everybody understands what that elevation to tier one means," he said.

In other news, France - well beaten by Samoa and England before playing out a World Cup classic against Lebanon - are expected to tour the southern hemisphere in 2027.

Grant also defended the IRL's decision to widen the game's international eligibility rules, allowing players to represent a country through the heritage of their great grandparent rather than grandparent.

"I think we have players sitting on the sidelines who the public deserve to see show their skills on the international stage," he said.
